Abstract
This report presents research on the relationship between the Kurux spoken in Nepal and the Kurux
spoken in India. The primary purpose of this research was to determine Nepali Kurux speakers’ level
of comprehension of the variety spoken in Jharkhand, India, and the ethnolinguistic perceptions of
these groups, with an aim to inform future language development activities.
    The research shows that the Kurux spoken in Nepal and in India should be considered varieties
of one language. They are linguistically similar, and comprehension in Nepal of the varieties from
Jharkhand and West Bengal is sufficiently high to be considered the same language (and share some
written materials). Furthermore, Nepali Kurux speakers see themselves as part of the wider
international Kurux community and have positive attitudes towards Kurux speakers in other places.
Language vitality in most Kurux-speaking communities in Nepal is high. A strong desire to read and
write in their language and the relatively strong language vitality makes the Nepali Kurux
community a good candidate for literacy and multilingual education programs. The Devanagari
orthography currently used by speakers in India is suitable to use for Nepali Kurux, but development
of materials in Nepal would be beneficial.

1 अनुवादक: मान जंग मगराती Translation: Man Jang Magarati

1     Introduction

The Kurux (Uranw) people of South Asia live in India, Nepal, Bangladesh, and Bhutan. The purpose
of this study, conducted in early 2018, was to better understand the sociolinguistic situation of Kurux
in Nepal, with a focus on the ethnolinguistic relationship between the Kurux community of Nepal
and that of India. While much research has been done on the Kurux language, until now no study has
sought to understand this relationship. There is much existing literature and other language materials
published in the Kurux language in India, and it was the aim of this study to provide information
that might aid in collaborative language development efforts between Kurux speakers in Nepal and
India.
    Both the Kurux language and its associated ethnic group have many names and alternate
spellings, which will be discussed. For the purposes of this report the term ‘Kurux’ will be used when
referring to the language and the language community. ‘Uranw’ will be used when referring
specifically to the ethnic group.
     This report begins with an introduction to the Kurux people and language and a review of
previous research on the Kurux language (Section 1). Following this is a description of the purpose
and goals of the study (Section 2), and the methodology used in the research (Section 3). Then the
results of the research are discussed, presenting findings on ethnolinguistic identity (Section 4),
linguistic variation and intelligibility results (Section 5), language development considerations
(Section 6), and language vitality status in Nepal (Section 7).
1.1     People
Multiple names have been used to refer to the Kurux language and its speakers in South Asia. These
names include ‘Kurux’, ‘Oraon’, ‘Dhangar’, ‘Jhangar’, and other variants. Because ‘Kurux’ is the
insider name for the language, in this report the term ‘Kurux’ is used for the language and for the
community of Kurux speakers in Nepal, India, and elsewhere. When referring specifically to the
ethnic group, ‘Uranw’ is used for the people in Nepal and ‘Oraon’ is used for the people in India. See
section 4.1 for further information on nomenclature.
1.1.1     Geography
Kurux is primarily spoken in India, Nepal, Bangladesh, and Bhutan, as displayed in map 1. For a
detailed map of the area where Kurux is spoken, see Appendix I.

     In India, Kurux is spoken primarily on the Chota Nagpur plateau, in the states of Jharkhand,
Chhattisgarh, and Odisha, with speakers also found in West Bengal, Assam, and Bihar.
    The population of Kurux speakers in India is 1,988,350 according to the 2011 census (Census of
India 2011). Approximately half of Indian Kurux speakers live in the state of Jharkhand, on the
Chota Nagpur plateau (formerly southern Bihar state) which is the Kurux homeland and is seen as
the core area of the Kurux people. Table 1 displays the number of Kurux speakers in the states of
India where they are most populous (Census of India 2011).

    The Kurux ethnicity is officially recognized by the Indian government under the name ‘Oraon’. It
is a Scheduled Tribe2 in the states of Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra,
Odisha, and West Bengal. The Kurux people of India reside in both rural and urban areas and are
highly influenced by Hindi and Sadri, as well as the Munda, Bengali, Maithili, Magahi, and Kurmali

languages (Yadava 2001). Despite this influence, the Kurux language continues to be widely used in
India.
    The Uranw, or Kurux people of Nepal live primarily in the Terai area of southeastern Nepal.
According to van Driem, the Kurux people in Nepal migrated in the mid-1800s from India and settled
near the Kosi river (2001:1029).
    Nepal is divided into seven provinces and seventy-seven districts. Nearly all Kurux in Nepal live
in Province 6 and Province 7, and over 60 percent of the population is concentrated in the district of
Sunsari. Map 2 displays the population distribution of Uranw speakers in Nepal.

    The vast majority of Uranw in Nepal live in rural, highly multilingual areas. However, it is
common for villages where Uranw people reside to be divided into homogenous neighborhoods. Even
though they live in ethnically mixed communities their homes are often in clusters of exclusively

Uranw people. Nepali is the dominant language in most of Nepal, and other common regional
languages in Uranw areas include Maithili, Tharu, Bhojpuri, Sadri, and Tamang.
    Bangladesh is also home to a significant Kurux population: about 50,000 people speak a variety
of Kurux in northwestern Bangladesh, in the Rangpur division (Ahmad et al. 2011). However, the
variety spoken in Bangladesh is quite different from that of Nepal and India (see section 1.2.3).
Kurux is also spoken in Bhutan by small group of approximately 4,200 Kurux speakers (Eberhard et
al. 2019).
1.1.2     History
The Kurux people of India did not always live in the northwestern portion of the Chota Nagpur
Plateau as they do today. According to Konow, drawing information from Gait’s writings in the
Report of the Census of Bengal 1901, the Kurux people migrated from their original home in
southeastern India, traveling up the Son river and settling in their current homeland in Jharkhand
(formerly southern Bihar) (1909). Kobayashi and Tirkey speculate that since there has been little
divergence of dialects within the Kurux language, this migration likely took place in “recent
centuries” (2017:10).
    Most sources indicate that the Uranw people of Nepal migrated north from the Chota Nagpur
region approximately 100 to 150 years ago (van Driem 2001, Gordon 1973, Kobayashi and Tirkey
2017). According to van Driem, “their forefathers were employed as indigo planters by the British in
the northern Bihar district of Purniya, whence they first crossed the border into the neighboring
Nepalese districts of Sunsari and Moran [sic].” (2001:1029) Although this is the generally accepted
history of the Uranw of Nepal, some Uranw people living in the central Terai regions claim their
ancestors were not migrants and their people group evolved in Nepal (Uranw et al. 2013:3).
1.1.3     Culture
While the Uranw of Nepal are culturally similar to many other ethnic groups residing in the Terai,
there are some notable differences, especially with regard to religious practices and celebrations.
Despite the influence of many other nearby ethnic groups, Uranw people maintain a strong sense of
their unique culture.
    Uranw home styles vary by area within Nepal, but are typically made of bamboo, mud, and cow
dung, with thatched roofs. Women often wear sarees and ornamental jewelry, but kurta suruwal and
even Western-style clothing are becoming common among younger women. Men traditionally wore
lungis, a cloth wrapped around the waist, but today middle-aged and younger men wear only
Western-style clothing.
    Most Uranw in Nepal are farmers by occupation, growing various grains, vegetables, and
tobacco, as well as keeping livestock. Many Uranw farmers are sharecroppers, and do not own their
own land. According to Bista (2004), some Uranw people also weave and sell bamboo baskets and
grain storage bins. Despite living in rural areas, even the most remote Uranw settlements have easy
access to major roads, larger towns, and cities. This allows for people to supplement farming with
other means of employment such as tailoring, metalworking, carpentry, technical jobs, office work,
and entrepreneurship.
    The Uranw social structure is fairly egalitarian. In his ethnographic overview People of Nepal,
Bista states that men and women in the Uranw community “enjoy equally important positions of
authority within the family,” dividing the domestic responsibilities between them (2004:156). He
also states that, traditionally, each Uranw settlement had its own leader or headman called maijan, to
whom most community members would appeal for legal and social disputes.
    Uranw people in Nepal have a unique religious tradition which centers around the festival
Karma Dharma, or Karam Festival. This festival is observed annually in late August or early
September and is celebrated through worship of branches of the Karam tree. The festival lasts two
days and consists of fasting, song and dance, and food offerings which are then eaten at the end of
the day to break the fast. Many Uranw people we met described the festival to us, citing it as an
essential element of their culture and religion. Yadava describes the festival in detail and writes that
its purpose is to bring wealth and prosperity in the coming year (2001:10). Uranw and Sapkota
describe the festival as a tribute to the god of wisdom and list other important festivals for Uranw
people such as the Jatara (new year) Festival in which joys and sorrows are celebrated, and the

5

Sukarati Festival in which the Uranw worship the goddess of wealth in their own unique way (2013).
The Uranw religion also has some influence from Hinduism, which is the dominant religion in Nepal,
and many Uranw people celebrate Hindu festivals such as Holi, Chaith, Cauthcand, Ghari, and
Dipawali (Yadava 2001:10). According to data gathered by Uranw and Sapkota (2013),
approximately 10 percent of Uranw people in Nepal practice Christianity, a statistic that was also
confirmed by the data gathered for this study.
    The Uranw people of Nepal have unique traditions associated with weddings and funerals as
well. Bista describes weddings in the Uranw community as a large, expensive affair, celebrated by
the whole village (2004:159). Our observations confirmed that Uranw weddings last multiple days
and include a party caravan in which the groom’s family travels to the bride’s home to retrieve her
for the ceremony and festivities. The Karam tree is also a central part of Uranw wedding traditions.
Bista also describes funerals, in which the Uranw bury the body and observe mourning for twelve
days. This period is terminated in a feast and purification rituals which include shaving of the head
for men and cutting of the nails for women (Bista 2004:159).
    For information on the culture of Oraon, or Kurux, in India, see The World of the Oraon (Ghosh
2006), The Religious History of Munda and Oraon Tribes (Miñja and Singh 2017), The Scheduled Tribes
(Singh 1994), and numerous other publications.
1.2     Language
The Kurux language is currently listed in the Ethnologue under two ISO 639-3 codes.3 The ISO code
for Kurux in India, Bangladesh, and Bhutan is [kru], and the ISO code for Kurux in Nepal is [kxl]
(Eberhard et al. 2019). Based on the findings of this study, we have requested that ISO 639-3 retire
the code [kxl] and combine it with the code [kru] because of the linguistic and sociolinguistic
evidence that these varieties should be defined as dialects of one language.
    Kurux belongs to the Dravidian family of languages and is often classified as Northern Dravidian
along with Malto and Brahui (Yadava and Turin 2006). In The Dravidian Languages, Krishnamurti
further classifies Kurux as Dravidian, Northern Dravidian, Kurux-Malto, Kurux (2003). However, as
stated by Kobayashi and Tirkey, “the position of Kurux-Malto in the family tree of Dravidian is a
difficult problem” (2017:11). They discuss that, while there are not firm grounds for the Northern
Dravidian subgrouping, Kurux does not belong with the other subgroupings of Dravidian.
    One reason Kurux is different from other Dravidian languages is the influence of surrounding
Indo-Aryan languages. Many authors mention this influence, including Gordon in his analysis of
clause patterns in Nepali Kurux. Gordon states that, while Kurux is indeed a Northern Dravidian
language, it also “…exhibits pervasively the affects [sic] of large-scale diffusion of Indo-Aryan
structural traits” and that “…Munda and Tibeto-Burman may have formed part of the network within
which this large-scale diffusion took place” (1973:37). Kobayashi and Tirkey, who based their
research in Jharkhand, India, discuss “extensive” lexical borrowing from Indo-Aryan languages, as
well as the presence of the phonemic glottal stop and complex verbal predicates and other signs of
Indo-Aryan influence (2017:14–15).
    The Kurux language has a total of thirty-four consonants,4 including contrastive aspiration, a
feature which is rare in Dravidian languages and may be another sign of Indo-Aryan influence. There
are twenty phonemic vowels in Kurux, including contrastive length and nasalization (Gordon 1976).
Linguists agree that Kurux in Nepal and India has SOV word order. Kobayashi and Tirkey discuss
features of Kurux such as suffixing morphology and noun agreement. They state that the Kurux verb
has three tenses, and expresses aspects with auxiliary verbs, and that the language has two genders
and six cases (2017).
    There has not been definitive research on the dialect situation of Kurux in India and Nepal.
Some researchers, such as Krishnamurti (2003:377), have speculated that the language in Nepal is a
separate language from that of India and Bangladesh. However, most sources do not address dialectal
variation within Kurux at all, while others list the language in Nepal as a dialect of Kurux. Kobayashi
and Tirkey include Nepal in a list of the dialects of Kurux (2017:10). Pike and Gordon (1972) also

1.2.1     India
Kurux in India is spoken in a relatively spread-out geographic area, from the ‘heartland’ of
Jharkhand to Chhattisgarh in the west, Odisha in the south, West Bengal in the north, with smaller
settlements as far east as Assam and Arunchal Pradesh. Despite the wide area in which speakers live,
Kurux has “a relatively uniform morphology” (Kobayashi and Tirkey 2017:9). However, most
linguists have indicated there are different dialects within India.
    To date, there have been no studies focused on defining the dialects of Kurux in India. Konow
asserted there were no dialects within Kurux, only that different groups used different loan words
from neighboring languages (1909). Kobayashi and Tirkey list some smaller areas near Ranchi which
have some variation between them but make no claims about the varieties outside of Jharkhand
(2017:10). The Kurux spoken in Jharkhand is generally accepted by linguists and Kurux speakers as
the central Indian variety and is the main area where Kurux writings and materials have been
published.
    The Kurux language in India has been developed for many years, and there is strong support for
continued production and promotion of Kurux materials. Extensive literature has been published
about the language and the people. Additionally, educational materials for all levels from elementary
to postgraduate have been published in the Kurux language. The language was officially recognized
by the government of Jharkhand in 2003 (Singh 2017) and is now used in some schools. Along with
educational materials, dictionaries, and linguistic materials, many other items have been published
by mother tongue speakers of Kurux, including plays, essays, collections of songs, novels, magazines,
journals, and more.
   A unique script called Tolong Siki was developed for Kurux in 1999, and this orthography was
formally recognized by the government in 2007 (Ager, n.d.). However, as this script takes some effort
to learn, a modified Devanagari script is more commonly used to write Kurux. This orthography
makes use of diacritics to mark features that are not represented in standard Devanagari script, such
as vowel length, nasal vowels, the phonemic glottal stop, and the uvular fricative. Roman script is
also sometimes used to write Kurux, especially with the ubiquity of mobile communication.5
    Because of the existing literature in the Kurux language, the EGIDS6 level of Kurux in India
could be categorized as EGIDS 5 (Developing), meaning that incipient literacy exists in the
community, but support is needed for it to become sustainable. However, based on the writings of
Kobayashi and Tirkey (2017) and others, and supported by our own observations, there is evidence
that the language in India is losing speakers. Our contacts in Ranchi reported that in rural areas the
language remains widely used, but in urban areas, fewer and fewer children are learning to speak
Kurux. Some people from Jharkhand mentioned that language vitality is higher in Chhattisgarh,
Bihar, and West Bengal.
    There have been some efforts to strengthen the vitality of the Kurux language such as planning
language society events for awareness raising, making materials such as Kurux promotional calendars
widely available, and organizing language promotion conferences. International Kurux conferences
have been hosted in India, Nepal, and Bangladesh.
1.2.2     Nepal
Kurux is the only Dravidian language spoken in Nepal and is highly influenced by the larger regional
languages in the areas where Kurux is spoken.
    There are differing opinions on the number of dialects within the Kurux language of Nepal. Van
Driem distinguishes two dialects of the language, calling them ‘Dhangar’ and ‘Jhangar’, aligning

them with the names used for the people living on the west and east sides of the Kosi river,
respectively (2001:1029).
    Uranw and Sapkota, in their sociolinguistic survey of Kurux in Nepal, identify three dialects
within Nepal. From dialect mapping and lexical similarity data, they propose a western dialect
spoken in Bara, Parsa, Rautahat, and Dhanusa districts, a geographically and linguistically central
dialect spoken in Sunsari, Morang, Siraha, Udayapur, Kathmandu, and Lalitpur districts, and an
eastern dialect spoken in Jhapa and Ilam districts (2013). According to their research, variance in the
manner of speaking and code switching as a result of language mixing with larger trade languages
are the main differences between these groups. For example, the way of speaking in Jhapa is
influenced by Sadri and Nepali. In Morang, Sunsari, and Siraha, the language is influenced by
Maithili and Nepali, and in Bara and Parsa, the language is influenced by Bhojpuri and Nepali.
According to the wordlist comparisons in this sociolinguistic survey, the lexical similarity between
the five Kurux sites tested ranged from 72 percent to 83 percent (Uranw and Sapkota 2013). This is
lower than the lexical similarity found in this study, which ranged from 84 percent to 92 percent (see
section 5.1 for a full explanation). Variation within Nepal is evident, but Kurux speakers and linguists
agree that the varieties of Kurux spoken in Nepal are one language.
    The vitality of the Kurux language in Nepal is currently high. Uranw and Sapkota’s survey of
Kurux in Nepal indicates strong language vitality, with high levels of intergenerational transfer and
positive language attitudes (2013). During this study, it was confirmed that language vitality in most
Kurux areas of Nepal is high, but the language is losing speakers overall.
1.2.3     Other varieties
The focus of this study was on Kurux as spoken in Nepal and India. This section addresses the other
Kurux varieties spoken in Bangladesh and Bhutan, as well as the related language Kisan; none of
these were investigated in this survey.
    The Ethnologue (Eberhard et al. 2019) currently classifies Kurux as spoken in Bhutan and
Bangladesh under the same ISO code [kru] as the Kurux spoken in India. There is very little
documentation on the Kurux spoken in Bhutan.
    According to a sociolinguistic survey of Kurux in Bangladesh (Ahmad et al. 2011), the language
there is significantly different from the Kurux spoken in India, partly because much of the vocabulary
is borrowed from Bangla. Like the Uranw of Nepal, the Kurux of Bangladesh migrated from the Chato
Nagpur area, and the adoption of many Bangla words into the Kurux vocabulary has caused the
language to diverge from modern Kurux in India (Ahmad et al. 2011).
    The data from this sociolinguistic survey showed little linguistic variation of Kurux within
Bangladesh. Lexical similarity ranged from 84 percent to 93 percent within Bangladesh. Lexical
similarity with Kurux spoken in Dima, West Bengal was much lower, ranging from 39 percent to 41
percent. The researchers propose that this low lexical similarity is a result of language mixing and
state, “Bangla forms a notable portion of the everyday vocabulary of Kurux people” (Ahmad et al.
2011:12). They also report that language vitality is weak and suggest the language may fall out of
use within one generation.
     In Bangladesh, there is also a sizeable population (166,000 according to the 2000 census) of
ethnically Oraon people who speak Sadri [sdr] (Eberhard et al. 2019). The Oraon people came from
India over 100 years ago and, sometime in the past, shifted from speaking Kurux to speaking Sadri,
an Indo-Aryan language (Cain 1988).
    The Kurux language is also related to Kisan (ISO code [xis]), which is a distinct Scheduled Tribe
in India. Kisan, which has an estimated 206,000 speakers (Census of India 2011) is primarily spoken
in the state of Odisha and has some speakers in Bihar and West Bengal. In a survey of the Kisan
completed in 1998, the lexical similarity between Kisan and Kurux spoken in Bihar and West Bengal
ranged from 46 to 74 percent. The survey also included intelligibility testing, with recorded text test
results ranging from 73 to 89 percent. In addition, the research showed a separate ethnolinguistic
identity between Kisan and Kurux (Bailey et. al. 1998).
1.3     Previous research
There has been much study of the Kurux language in both Nepal and India, but there is no
substantiated information on the relationship between the two varieties.

8

    Some of the earliest linguistic work on Kurux in India was produced by Ferdinand Hahn, a
Lutheran minister. His work was based in Ranchi, and he published a grammar (1900), dictionary
(1903), and “Kurukh” folk stories (1905). Grignard, a Jesuit priest who collaborated with Hahn, after
many years of study, published an early grammar (1926) and a dictionary of the “Oraon” language in
India (1924). Konow, whose early surveys of the Munda and Dravidian languages of India were
published in Linguistic Survey of India, provides population data for Kurux people in India and a
grammar sketch, and notes that, while his data came from the Ranchi area, he found no variation in
the language in different regions of India (1909).
    There are several dictionaries of the Kurux spoken in India, including An English-Oraon
Dictionary, which was begun by Grignard and published posthumously (Bleses 1956). The most
recent lexicography from India is a Kurux-Hindi dictionary published in 1979 (Prasad).
    Ekka published a descriptive study of Kurux in Ranchi in 1972 and later published a Kurux
phonetic reader (1985). Two separate works on Kurux historical phonology were published in India
by Pinnow (1964) and Pfeiffer (1972).
     In the 1970s, Gordon published various grammatical and phonological analyses of Kurux,
including an article on non-transitive clause structures (Pike and Gordon 1972), an article on clause
patterns (Gordon 1973), and a thorough phonological analysis (Gordon 1976). Most of their research
was based on data collected in Sunsari and Morang districts in Nepal, but the phonology also
includes some information from Ranchi.
    Van Driem, in his work Languages of the Himalayas, discusses the history of the Kurux peoples
and includes some information on the “Uraon” in Nepal (2001:1029).
    More recently, works on Kurux have been published which focus on the people and language in
Nepal, such as Yadav’s 1999 sociolinguistic profile of the “Dhangar” in Siraha, Nepal. In 2004,
Bhandari and Sita published an introduction to “Uranw” language and culture in Nepal.
    Yadava (2001) published a preliminary study of the “Dhangar” language (Kurux in Siraha,
Nepal), which includes a brief grammar sketch and sociolinguistic study. Other recent linguistic
research in Nepal includes a grammar sketch of the “Jhangar” language (Sapkota 2006), a study of
the non-finite clauses of “Dhangar” language (Yadav 2005), and an M.A. thesis on verb morphology
of Kurux in Nepal (Uranw 2008).
    The most recent study on Kurux in Nepal is a 2013 sociolinguistic report by Uranw and Sapkota
of Tribhuvan University. Their study, which took place in Jhapa, Morang, Sunsari, Siraha, and Bara
districts, includes information about the history and customs of the Uranw people, as well as in-depth
discussions of domains of language use and multilingualism, language attitudes, language vitality,
language resources, and linguistic variation within Nepal.
    Along with linguistic and sociolinguistic information, there are many other resources available
regarding the Kurux language and people. In India, there are textbooks written about and in the
Kurux language, as well as a myriad of books and articles available describing the Oraon people and
culture. “Kurukh World” is a useful online resource about Kurux peoples and language. In the Kurux
language itself there are plays, magazines, novels, poems, songs, and much more, mostly published in
Jharkhand, India.
    While some previous works on the Kurux language have speculated about the relationship
between the varieties spoken in Nepal and India, no research has produced data on this subject. Most
works were produced in either Nepal or India, and to date there are no comparisons that have been
done between the Kurux spoken in India and the Kurux spoken in Nepal. Therefore, this study
focuses on the lexical relationship, levels of intelligibility, and ethnolinguistic relationship between
Kurux in Nepal and India, with an aim to provide information that would assist collaborative
language development efforts.
2     Purpose, goals, and research questions

The purpose of this research was to obtain an understanding of the sociolinguistic situation of the
Kurux language and people in Nepal, with a focus on their relationship with Kurux in India. In order
to accomplish this, data was gathered on the linguistic relationship as well as the ethnolinguistic
attitudes among the different varieties of Kurux, with the aim of assessing the possibility for Nepali
Kurux communities to use existing materials from India as well as recommending activities for
further language development in Nepal. The following sections state the goals of the study, with
research questions and tools utilized to answer each question.

9

2.1     Goal 1: Ethnolinguistic identity and attitudes assessment
Understand the ethnolinguistic relationship between Kurux in Nepal and Kurux in India.
•  Do Kurux speakers in Nepal perceive themselves to be part of the international Kurux
    ethnolinguistic community? (Knowledgeable insider interviews, individual interviews, dialect
   mapping, post-story questions, observation)
•  What are the attitudes of Nepali Kurux towards the Kurux language and people in India?
    (Knowledgeable insider interviews, individual interviews, dialect mapping, post-story questions,
    observation)
•  What are the patterns of contact between the Kurux communities in Nepal and India?
    (Knowledgeable insider interviews, individual interviews, dialect mapping, post-story questions,
    observation)
2.2     Goal 2: Linguistic variation and comprehension assessment
Determine the level of comprehension between the varieties of Kurux in Nepal and India through
emic perspective (that of the speakers themselves), lexical similarity, and comprehension testing.
•  What is the lexical relationship among the varieties of Kurux in Nepal, Jharkhand, and West
    Bengal? (Wordlist Comparisons)
•    Is the Kurux spoken in India intelligible to Kurux speakers in Nepal? (Recorded text testing and
    story playing)
•  What is the perceived comprehension of different varieties of the Kurux language by speakers in
    Nepal? (Knowledgeable insider interviews, individual interviews, dialect mapping)
2.3     Goal 3: Language development needs assessment
Assess the potential for literature available in Indian Kurux to be used in Nepal and understand the
factors influencing language development decisions in Nepal.
•    Is the existing Kurux orthography used in India acceptable to and easily understood by Kurux
    speakers in Nepal? (Orthography test, knowledgeable insider interviews)
•  Do speakers in Nepal have access to currently existing Kurux materials? (Knowledgeable insider
    interviews, individual interviews, orthography test, observation)
•  What goals do Nepali Kurux communities express for language-based development?
    (Knowledgeable insider interviews, individual interviews)
2.4     Goal 4: Vitality assessment
Evaluate the language vitality of selected Kurux speech communities in Nepal.
•  What is the current language vitality of Kurux in Nepal, as indicated by patterns of language use,
    motivating factors, and support for acquisition? (Knowledgeable insider interviews, individual
    interviews, observation)
3    Methodology

The main research for this study was conducted by three researchers (Sarah Shackelford, Janel
Swenson, and Ram Chaudhary) over the course of two fieldwork trips in January–February 2018: the
first to Jharkhand, India, and the second to four sites in Nepal. A Kurux guide, Sampat Lal Uranw,
accompanied us to the sites in Nepal. Additional data was gathered in West Bengal by Loren
Maggard.
3.1     Instruments
The following instruments were administered using Nepali, the target language, and/or other
languages as appropriate. The instruments were translated into Nepali and pilot tested prior to being
used in fieldwork. Full descriptions of each tool can be found in the appendices of this report.

10

3.1.1     Wordlist comparisons
Description and purpose: Wordlists of 338 items are compared to estimate the degree of lexical
similarity between the speech varieties the wordlists represent.
Procedure: Wordlists were elicited from mother-tongue speakers of each speech variety using Nepali
or English and were transcribed by the researchers using the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA).
A lexical similarity analysis was carried out on each pair of wordlists.
Advantages: Data collection is relatively efficient. Wordlists can provide broad insights into possible
dialect groupings.
Disadvantages: Wordlists can only confirm low levels of intelligibility between speech varieties
compared. They cannot give conclusive evidence regarding high levels of intelligibility.
    Appendix B contains more information on this tool, including details of the analysis of the data.
3.1.2     Recorded text test (RTT) and post-story questions
Description and purpose: The subjects listen to recorded stories from other varieties with
comprehension questions inserted. After the subject hears the story and answers comprehension
questions, they are asked questions regarding language attitudes and dialect perceptions. This tool
assesses the subjects’ actual understanding of speech from various areas along with gathering
information about their attitudes towards and perceptions of the samples of speech.
Procedure: A narrative story was collected from a native speaker of Kurux in Jharkhand, India. This
story was then played for people in Uranw communities in Nepal, who were not told where the
sample of speech was recorded. As subjects listened to the story a second time, they orally answered
comprehension questions (recorded in their own variety) about the story. After listening to each
story, the subjects answered questions about their perceived understanding of and opinions toward
the speech variety used by the storyteller. After the RTT was administered, a second narrative story
from West Bengal, India was played for the respondents. No comprehension questions were asked7,
but the subjects were asked about their perceived understanding of and opinions toward the speech
variety used by the storyteller in this second story.
Advantages: By using actual samples of speech from a selected variety, an initial assessment of
comprehension and attitudes can be made. RTTs allow someone who is not fluent in the language
under study to administer a dialect intelligibility test.
Disadvantages: RTT results, while helpful, only evaluate basic understanding of spoken language and
are not a direct measure of intelligibility between two varieties. RTTs do not measure reading or
writing ability in another variety. RTTs can be time consuming and complicated to develop, and the
reliability of results are affected by many variables that can be difficult for the researcher to control.
    Appendix C contains more information on the development and administration of this tool, as
well as information on considerations for interpretating the results.
3.1.3     Knowledgeable insider interviews
Description and purpose: A member of the community who is viewed as knowledgeable regarding
information about their language is interviewed with prepared questions. This tool provides
information about the language and community from a reliable and knowledgeable source.
Procedure: An interview schedule was developed by researchers and was administered to one or two
people at each site. Questions ranged from specific population estimates and locations of speakers to
general information about vitality and multilingualism within the community.
7 Comprehension questions were not asked in the West Bengal story because (1) Jharkhand was the main
reference dialect under study, as it is the main dialect with developed literature, and (2) the researchers were
unable to travel to West Bengal for the development and testing of a full RTT.

11

Advantages: A great deal of information can be gathered in a relatively efficient manner. This tool
also shows respect to important members of the community.
Disadvantages: Questionnaires are only administered to one or two people at each research site, and
thus the results may not be representative of the whole community.
    Appendix F contains the full interview schedule and responses.
3.1.4      Individual interviews
Description and purpose: Native speakers of the language are interviewed using a prepared list of
questions. This guides interaction in order to gather information regarding specific sociolinguistic
issues. It also allows freedom to deviate from the interview schedule if such extra discussion provides
additional information relevant to the research questions of the study.
Procedure: An interview schedule was designed by the researchers to obtain the type of information
needed to answer the research questions. It was then administered to a representative sample of
speakers in each site. Interviews were conducted one-on-one, with questions asked orally by the
researcher, and the subject’s responses were recorded in a notebook. The same questions were asked
of each subject, and follow-up questions were asked when appropriate.
Advantages: Depending on the length of the interview, the time in administration is not extensive,
which allows for many individuals to be interviewed. The flexible nature of the interview helps the
respondents feel comfortable and share openly, while allowing the interviewer to explore topics in
greater depth and seek context for certain responses.
Disadvantages: Individual interviews are limited in that subjects might only report what they want the
researcher to hear, or what they believe the researcher would like to hear.
    Appendix E contains the full interview schedule and responses.
3.1.5      Dialect mapping
Description and purpose: Dialect mapping is a Participatory Methods tool. The purpose of Participatory
Methods is to gain an insider perspective from a group of community members regarding their
perceptions of the situation of their language. This method differs from interviews in that the
procedure is collaborative in nature, allowing for input from all community members and resulting in
collective data. The dialect mapping tool encourages discussion of the community’s perspectives
regarding dialects, the geographic location of each, and perceived levels of comprehension between
varieties.
Procedure: Participants were invited to create a physical diagram describing their linguistic landscape
by identifying and mapping out other locations where their language is spoken. They then were
asked to identify any groupings within the language. Each of these groups was then classified by the
participants’ level of understanding of each group, the amount of difference they perceive between
their variety and each of the other varieties, and their perspectives and attitudes towards those
varieties.
Advantages: This method provides a visual representation of the speech communities with which the
participants interact, how well they feel they understand the speech in those communities, and their
attitudes towards the speech of those communities. It allows participants to collaborate and
appreciate their collective knowledge.
Disadvantages: The process may seem complicated or repetitive to the participants. In some
situations, participants may acquiesce to the opinions of a few outspoken individuals. Additionally,
insider perspectives do not always match linguistic reality, as perceptions can often be based on
hearsay.
    Appendix G contains the discussion schedule and responses for this tool.

12

3.1.6     Orthography test
Description and purpose: Native speakers are asked to read aloud a sample of text written in another
variety of their language. The orthography test is meant to determine whether a writing system
developed in another variety of the language is suitable for the variety in question.
Procedure: Subjects who were known to have a certain level of literacy in Nepali were asked to read
aloud a selection of text from a story from Jharkhand, India, written in Devanagari script. They were
assessed on the degree of ease with which they read the text and were asked comprehension
questions to test their comprehension of the text. Subjects also answered questions about their
perceived understanding of the story and their opinions toward the speech variety in the text.
Advantages: Orthography testing gives a preliminary understanding of how well speakers of one
variety can understand the writing system developed in another area. It may also identify areas of
potential difficulty in adapting existing materials into a new variety.
Disadvantages: Orthography testing uses a short piece of text which may not be representative of all
materials that have been developed in the language. Additionally, subjects may not be accustomed to
reading in their own language, and so difficulties in reading the text may be due to factors other than
suitability of the orthography or language in the text.
    Appendix D contains more information about this tool, including the tested text, interview
schedule, and responses.
3.1.7     Observation
Description and purpose: Researchers make notes of their observations at each site based on a list of
specific topics such as the behavior of people, the linguistic situation, and the material culture.
Procedure: The researchers intentionally observed each topic on the observation schedule, taking
notes in each site visited.
Advantages: Information collected though observation can be used to corroborate or contradict the
findings of other tools used during the survey. Additionally, researchers may be able to identify
behavioral trends that the subjects themselves may not be aware of.
Disadvantages: Observations may be limited by the researchers’ levels of language proficiency and
degree of cultural understanding. Other limitations are the relatively short amount of time spent at
each site and the fact that people may behave differently when an outsider is near (observer’s
paradox).

   Two areas were visited in India: Ranchi/Lohardaga in Jharkhand and Pathibari in West Bengal.8
The Ranchi area was chosen as the main reference site for the RTT development and wordlist
collection, with tools development also taking place in the nearby district of Lohardaga. The
Jharkhand region is considered a core area for the Kurux population in India and is the area where
the most language development in Kurux has occurred. Pathibari, West Bengal was selected as a
second reference site in India, as background research indicated the language there is different from
the language in Jharkhand, and the relationship between Kurux in Nepal and West Bengal was
unknown. In West Bengal, a wordlist was elicited, and a story was recorded for playing in Nepal.
   A total of four sites were visited in Nepal. Site selection in Nepal was guided by the following:
1) sites which reflect different regions where Kurux is spoken to represent linguistic diversity, 2) sites
where high language vitality was expected, and 3) sites where large numbers of people identify
themselves as Uranw. Two central sites were visited: Bhokraha (Bhokraha GP,9 Sunsari) and Lochani
(Sundar Haraicha NP,10 Morang). These villages are both in the area of Nepal with the highest
concentration of Kurux speakers. Two periphery sites were also visited: Tokla Tea Farm (Mechinagar
NP, Jhapa) and Siddhapur (Sakhuwa Prasauni GP, Parsa). These areas are less densely populated,
and background research indicated the people there speak different varieties of the Kurux language.
     All tools were administered in each of the research sites in Nepal, with the exception of Tokla.
Upon arrival in Tokla, we discovered it is a migrant community made up of a variety of peoples

4     Ethnolinguistic identity and attitudes

A key factor in understanding the boundaries between languages is the identity and attitudes of the
speakers themselves. This study sought to discover the perspectives of the Kurux people in Nepal,
regarding their ethnolinguistic identity and perceived relationship with the Kurux in India.
    According to the findings of this study, Kurux people have a strong ethnolinguistic identity and
include all Kurux speakers in this group. However, because of geographic distance and low levels of
contact between the varieties in Nepal and India, their identity is less cohesive with Kurux speakers
from more distant regions. Multiple names are recognized for the Kurux community, but lack of clear
consensus on a preferred name does not weaken their shared sense of identity. Contact between
Kurux speakers in Nepal and Kurux speakers in Jharkhand and other parts of India is minimal, but
Kurux speakers have generally positive attitudes towards other varieties of their language. Speakers
in Nepal also had enthusiastically positive attitudes towards actual samples of speech from
Jharkhand and West Bengal, further supporting that these groups have a unified ethnolinguistic
identity.
4.1     Nomenclature
Commonly recognized names can strengthen a community’s unity as one defined group. As was
mentioned in the introduction, various names have been used for the Kurux language and
community, both by insiders and by outsiders.
     In Nepal, the autoglottonym (internal name) for this language and ethnic group is [kuɽukʰa] or
[kuɽkʰa], often Romanized as ‘Kurukha’, ‘Kudukha’, or ‘Khurkha’, and written in Devanagari as ‘खुडुखा’,
‘कुड़्ख़ा’, or ‘खुखार्’, among other spellings. During this study, this internal name was mentioned in
interviews, dialect mapping sessions, and other conversations. Some people were observed using the
name “Kurukha” when speaking in Kurux, and the name “Uranw” when speaking in Nepali.
    The term ‘Kurux’14 ([kuɽuχ]), written “कुड़ुख़” in Devanagari, is listed by many sources as the term
preferred by the people themselves. According to the data gathered by Uranw and Sapkota in their
recent survey of Kurux in Nepal, more than 90 percent of people surveyed expressed a preference for
‘Kurux’ as the name for both their ethnic group and their language (2013:5–13). The data gathered
for this study also revealed a preference for ‘Kurux’ as the language name, although with less
consistency, and indicated that ‘Uranw’ is more commonly designated as the preferred caste name.
    The term ‘Uranw’15 ([uɾãũ̯]), written “उराँव” in Devanagari, is the commonly used surname in this
group in Nepal. Uranw is also the language name registered in the Nepal census data (Central Bureau
of Statistics 2011), and this name has been used in many publications to refer to the Uranw people.
Some members of the community asserted that the name ‘Uranw’ is a newer name, and while it is not
the internal name for the group, it is generally accepted by people in Nepal.
    The terms ‘Dhangar’ (धागढ) and ‘Jhangar’16 (झागाड्) are also sometimes used to refer to the Uranw
people and language in Nepal and are commonly found in older literature on the language. In the
most recent census, the government designates “Jhangad/Dhagar” as the name for the Uranw ethnic
group (Central Bureau of Statistics 2011). According to various sources, the Uranw people living west
of the Kosi river in Nepal are called ‘Dhangar’, while those east of the river are called ‘Jhangar’. This
delineation is also used by some linguists to denote a dialect boundary for the Kurux language

were given to the group by outsiders forty to sixty years ago and are seen as outdated and pejorative.
     In summary, while there is not complete consensus within the community in Nepal, ‘Uranw’ and
‘Kurux’ are both acceptable names for the language and people group. ‘Uranw’ is the most commonly
accepted outsider name for the ethnic group, is the surname used by nearly all in the community and
is the officially recognized name of the language. Both ‘Kurux’ and ‘Uranw’ are used by the
community for their language, with preference for one name over the other varying throughout
Nepal and across generations. The autoglottonym, or internal name, for the language and community
in Nepal and India is ‘Kurukha’. In India, the term ‘Kurukh’ is typically used for the language, and
‘Oraon’ is the official name for the ethnic group. While these terms are spelled differently, their
pronunciation is the same as those used in Nepal, and thus, for simplicity’s sake, the spelling ‘Kurux’
is used throughout this report.
    The term ‘Uranw’ is used in this report when referring specifically to the ethnic group in Nepal,
and ‘Oraon’ is used for the ethnic group in India. Because ‘Kurux’ is the insider name for the
language and because of the unified ethnolinguistic identity of Kurux speakers in Nepal and India,
the term ‘Kurux’ is used in this report for the language and for the community of Kurux speakers in
Nepal and across all countries.
4.2      Ethnolinguistic identity
Due to the multiple names used for the Kurux language and people, along with the geographic
distance between the various locations where Kurux people live (i.e., Nepal and various places in
India), one focus of this research was understanding the ethnolinguistic identity of these groups.
While the historic connection between these varieties is clear, little research has been done regarding
the current relationship between the geographically divided Kurux groups.
     In this study, the data indicate that Kurux people in Nepal see themselves as part of the
international Kurux ethnolinguistic community. Most of the interview respondents had met someone
from India (73%), and all of these expressed their own variety of Kurux was one language with that
of places such as Bihar, Jharkhand, and West Bengal. In other tools such as dialect mapping and
interviews with knowledgeable insiders, Kurux speakers were asked to list places where their
language is spoken. In these situations, most people focused first on nearby Kurux areas but, when
asked about India, they were comfortable with including even less well known Kurux places such as
Assam, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, and Arunachal Pradesh.

18

    The aims of this study did not allow for extensive research among Kurux speakers in India, but
the limited information that was gathered in Jharkhand indicates that Kurux speakers in India have
similarly inclusive ethnolinguistic perceptions. Kurux people in Jharkhand have a very strong
language identity, and despite often being well-traveled, maintain a close connection to their home
language and culture. Those we met confidently described Kurux people in Nepal as part of the
Kurux language and ethnic group.
     In summary, Kurux speakers in Nepal regard all Kurux speakers in India and elsewhere as part
of their ethnolinguistic group, and Kurux speakers in both Nepal and India have a strong sense of
identity.
4.3     Language attitudes
This study sought to understand the attitudes of Kurux speakers in Nepal towards the different
varieties of their language in order to determine the potential for the possibility of sharing literature
among the Kurux in both India and Nepal. Overall, Kurux speakers are enthusiastic about their
language and proud of being Uranw. In both India and Nepal, we observed positive language
attitudes and met people who expressed interest in all things related to their language and culture.
     Before examining Kurux speakers’ perspectives towards other varieties of their language, it is
important to understand the levels of contact between the different groups. Observations and
interview data indicated the level of contact between Kurux speakers in Nepal and more distant
regions of India is low. Although a majority of interview respondents had met Kurux speakers from
India,18 most had only met people from northern Bihar, where the language is reportedly very similar
to their own. Only 12 percent of all interviewees had met someone from Jharkhand, and only 4
percent had met someone from West Bengal. The data gathered from other tools confirmed that few
Kurux speakers in Nepal had met Kurux speakers from India, and even fewer had heard of or seen
any written materials in the Kurux language.

perceptions of the language there, and no one expressed negative opinions. Table 5 shows responses

5     Linguistic variation and comprehension

One main goal of this study was to determine the ability of Kurux speakers in Nepal to understand
the Kurux language as spoken in Jharkhand and elsewhere in India. Several tools provided insight
into the linguistic variation between Nepal and India. We used wordlist comparisons to understand
the relationship between the varieties, recorded text tests (RTTs) to gather data on intelligibility, and
dialect mapping and interviews to understand Kurux speakers’ perspectives.
    The Kurux language in Nepal is clearly one language with the Kurux language spoken in
Jharkhand and elsewhere in India. Lexical similarity results provide evidence that the varieties of
Kurux in Nepal are very similar. When comparing the varieties in Nepal with the Indian varieties in
Jharkhand and West Bengal, lexical similarity results were lower, but not significantly so. In
conjunction with the lexical similarity results, relatively high RTT results and positive attitudes
expressed by respondents towards the story from Jharkhand support the conclusion that
comprehension of the language from Jharkhand is high, and that speakers perceive it to be their own
language. Perceived comprehension of the story from West Bengal was similarly high, although the
language was seen to be different from the Jharkhand story. Data from dialect mapping and
interviews also support the conclusion that Kurux in India and Nepal is one unified language.

20

5.1      Lexical relationship (wordlist comparisons)
Wordlist comparisons are a useful tool for assessing the linguistic relatedness of speech varieties and
gaining a preliminary understanding of dialect groupings within a language. Lists of lexical items are
elicited from speakers in selected areas. These items are then compared to determine how many are
pronounced the same or similarly to items from another variety. The number of similar items
between each variety is then calculated, resulting in a lexical similarity percentage. For this study,
338 lexical items were elicited, and the method outlined by Blair (1990) was used to compare the
data. (See Appendix B for more information.)
    The goal of this study was not to understand the historical relationship between these Kurux
varieties, as there is ample evidence of the Kurux people’s migration to Nepal within the last few
hundred years. Rather, the goal of this research was to understand current levels of intelligibility,
and thus certain items that may typically be excluded (such as borrowed words and morphology)
were included in the lexical similarity analysis. Because of this methodology, the percentages seen
here are likely a conservative estimate.19 Table 7 shows the results of the wordlist comparison.

    According to Blair (1990:63), if two varieties have a lexical similarity of greater than 60
percent, intelligibility testing must be done. Joseph Grimes, in his paper on “Correlations between
vocabulary similarity and intelligibility” (1992), confirms this. In studying the correlation between
similarity in vocabulary and intelligibility of 55 dialect pairs in the Philippines, he found that for
lexical similarity above 60 percent there was a wide range of intelligibility scores (as measured by
RTTs), signifying a low level of correlation. Thus, the lexical similarity percentages between these
Kurux varieties indicate that intelligibility testing and other data are needed to better understand
how well Kurux speakers in Nepal can understand the Kurux language spoken in India.
5.2       Intelligibility testing and story playing
In order to understand how well Kurux speakers in Nepal comprehend the Kurux language spoken in
India, information from intelligibility testing and reported comprehension were examined. The
resulting data confirms that Kurux speakers in Nepal can comprehend the varieties from both
Jharkhand and West Bengal well, but not perfectly. Respondents perceived linguistic differences from
their own variety and between the two stories but expressed positive attitudes towards both stories.

      It should be noted that some linguists define ‘intelligibility’ as inherent, often theoretical,
understanding of another speech variety, while ‘comprehension’ or ‘understanding’ is used to refer to
learned or actual understanding of another variety, often synonymous with ‘bilingualism’. Separating
these concepts in actuality is not straightforward or simple and, in this case, does not add to our
understanding of the language situation. Therefore in this study the terms intelligibility,
comprehension, and understanding are all used to refer to the same concept—how well one person
can understand another person’s speech.
5.2.1     Recorded text tests: Procedure and review
A recorded text test (RTT), also known as dialect intelligibility test, was used to ascertain how well
Kurux speakers in Nepal are able to comprehend the language spoken in Jharkhand, India. This area
was chosen as a reference site in India because of the large amount of existing Kurux materials from
that area and because of a desire to understand whether these materials could be used by Kurux
speakers in Nepal. A story was recorded from a Kurux speaker near Ranchi in the state of Jharkhand,
pilot tested in the Jharkhand area, and then tested in three sites in Nepal.
    The testing procedure began with a short sample story recorded in the subject’s local variety.
Subjects who correctly answered most questions about the first story then listened to the Jharkhand
story straight through once. They then heard the story a second time with comprehension questions
inserted at appropriate points in the story.
   A second story, recorded in Pathibari in the state of West Bengal, India, was also played for
subjects, but without comprehension questions inserted. After each story, subjects answered
questions which gave context to provide more information about the perceived understanding and
language attitudes of Kurux speakers in Nepal towards the language in India.
     In order to understand the RTT results, three numbers and their significance must be
understood. The first is the average score, which is the mean or average of all subjects’ scores in a
single site. Each individual score is a percentage of correct answers out of a total possible 10 or 11.20
Average scores below 60 percent are generally considered to indicate inadequate comprehension.
Casad performed a study correlating average RTT scores with reported comprehension in which
varieties with RTT scores of 75–90 percent were found to be considered “easy” or sufficiently
intelligible by speakers (1974:83–86). It should be emphasized that a mean score of 70 percent, for
example, does not indicate that speakers of one variety can understand 70 percent of the variety
being tested. Rather, it allows the researchers to make an inference about probable levels of
understanding between the groups.
    The second important figure is standard deviation, which is a measure of how much individual
scores vary from the overall average. If most subjects score similarly, the standard deviation will be
low. If some subjects do well on the test and others do poorly, the standard deviation will be high.
For RTTs a standard deviation of 12–15 percent and above is typically considered high, and 10–12
percent or below is considered low.
    The third factor that is important for interpreting RTT scores is subject selection and sample
size. As discussed in section 3.3, for this study a convenience sample stratified for gender and age
was used. Testing a variety of subjects is important for accuracy of the overall average and the
standard deviation.
    These figures, when taken together and interpreted appropriately, can give insight into the
intelligibility relationship between the varieties of a language. Blair presents the relationship
between average score and standard deviation, shown here in table 8 (1990:25).

    Often when interpreting intelligibility testing results, the discussion of inherent intelligibility
versus learned intelligibility (bilingualism) is raised. In theory, the two are quite separate, but in
practice. it can be very difficult to parse them. Casad, in his notable study, Dialect Intelligibility Testing

therefore, any qualified subject should accurately represent the whole. Therefore, a high standard
deviation is traditionally interpreted to indicate that learned intelligibility has affected the
performance of some test subjects, and therefore the RTT scores are not an accurate reflection of
intelligibility. However, high standard deviations may result from a variety of variables, as has been
argued by O’Leary (1994), Yoder (2017), and others. Variables such as the subject’s performance, the
number of questions, the subject matter of the text, inconsistent test administration, translation
issues, etc., are also contributing factors to variation in test scores.
    Some researchers attempt to control for learned intelligibility or other factors by excluding
subjects with high levels of contact with other varieties, but because of the highly multilingual
situation in Nepal this is not feasible. Rather than controlling for certain factors, this research
attempted to gather a sample representative of the population under study.
     Despite these limitations to what RTT data can tell us, the RTT is still one of the most rigorous
sociolinguistic tests for intelligibility. A major benefit of the RTT as a comprehension test is that the
researcher need not understand the language under study, and it does not require a speaker of the
tested variety to be physically present. Also, unlike other intelligibility tests which focus on
production, the RTT focuses on comprehension. Despite its limitations, RTT data helps create a
clearer picture of the relationship between language varieties and the potential for comprehension
between them.

5.2.3    Summary of intelligibility testing results
Among the Kurux speakers tested in Nepal, the RTT results show sufficiently high comprehension of
the story from Jharkhand at 86 percent, with a standard deviation of 11 percent. The results
demonstrate some variation in understanding across the sites, but the lowest (83% in Sunsari) is still
adequately high. Older people and younger people scored similarly on the test, while men scored
slightly higher than women. While this is not a direct measure of the ability of Nepali Kurux speakers
to understand the variety spoken in Jharkhand, it is an indicator that actual levels of comprehension
are likely to be high.
    Kurux speakers’ attitudes towards the Jharkhand story and the West Bengal story were positive,
despite perceiving the speech varieties represented by the stories to be a little different. People gave
similar responses to questions about the two stories. Young respondents had less confidence than
older people in their comprehension of the stories, but the majority of respondents in both groups
felt they understood both stories well, and there was not a clear consensus on which story was easier
to understand. Most respondents could not identify where the language in each story was from.

5.3     Perceived comprehension of Kurux varieties
Along with data such as that from the analysis of lexical similarity and the results of dialect
intelligibility testing, the perceptions of Kurux speakers were a key source of information regarding
levels of comprehension of the different varieties spoken in Nepal and India. Speakers’ opinions were
elicited through community discussions (dialect mapping), interviews, informal conversations, and
observation. Most Kurux speakers perceive some linguistic variation within their language in Nepal,
but do not find these differences prohibitive to comprehension. There is not a strong consensus
within Nepal on which Kurux variety is easiest to understand, although the varieties in India are seen
as more different than other varieties in Nepal and neighboring northern Bihar.
    Respondents in Nepal were asked for their opinions on linguistic differences between different
varieties of Kurux in individual interviews and knowledgeable insider interviews. Each participant
was asked if they had met Kurux speakers from India and from the three most different places in
Nepal (Sunsari district, Parsa district, and Jhapa district22), and how well they understood the
language spoken by people there. Nearly every respondent who had met someone from these places
reported being able to comprehend all of the Kurux spoken there, with the exception of the speech
from Jharkhand, which received mixed responses. Some linguistic differences were acknowledged,
but all respondents reported the other varieties of Kurux in Nepal and India are at most “a little
different” from their own variety.
     Dialect mapping was also relied upon for gathering information on speakers’ perceptions of
variation within Kurux. Dialect mapping is a tool that allows researchers to facilitate a community
discussion about language variation and use. For this study, three dialect mapping sessions were
organized in Nepal, in Sunsari (Bhokraha), Morang (Lochani), and Parsa (Siddhapur). Each
community was guided through the process of creating a map of the Kurux language area: writing
locations where their language is spoken, arranging these locations into groups, ranking the groups
by their similarity to the local variety, and more. (For a complete description of the tool and the
results, see Appendix G.) These sessions give insight into the perspectives of the speakers themselves
with regard to linguistic variation within their group.
    The Uranw people are inclusive; they recognize all Kurux speakers, no matter the country, as
part of their ethnolinguistic group. When asked to list locations where their language is spoken, the
community gave much attention to listing nearby areas, but once they were prompted to list further
areas, in all three sessions the participants included Jharkhand and other states in India.
    There was not a clear consensus on how well each group could understand people from other
Kurux-speaking areas, yet some patterns emerged. In all three sessions, participants reported they can
understand all of the Kurux language spoken in the districts of Sunsari, Morang, and Saptari, and in
places in Bihar near their own location. All other places in Nepal that were mentioned were indicated
as being completely or mostly understood, with little to no need to modify their way of speaking
when communicating with Kurux speakers in Nepal and Bihar. Some mentioned that, in various
areas of Nepal, people mix their language with larger regional languages, but that communication
with them is still possible. The exception to this is Jhapa, which the groups from Parsa and Morang
listed as very different and stated that communication in Kurux with them can be difficult or even
impossible. This could be due to low vitality, language mixing, or the fact that Kurux speakers in
Jharkhand migrated there from distant places in India.
     Participants were less confident in their opinions of the Kurux spoken in India further than
neighboring Bihar. Most participants had not met speakers from the more distant places, so in each
site a few knowledgeable people were relied on for the information. All three groups considered
themselves separate from Jharkhand and other places in India (excluding Bihar). In Parsa and
Sunsari, people listed Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh/West Bengal as the most difficult to understand.
In Morang, the group listed west Indian states (Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, West Bengal) and Jhapa
as the most difficult to understand. Most indicated that they are able to use their own language with
people in Jharkhand, but there were mixed opinions on whether Nepali Kurux speakers need to use a
regional language to communicate with people who speak varieties from other states in India. One

   When asked where the best location for language development would be, no one place was
agreed on as the most prestigious or best place for language development, but all groups agreed that
speakers within Nepal and Bihar could share Kurux language materials. Despite non-negative
attitudes towards the language in Jharkhand, Nepali Kurux speakers recognize enough linguistic
differences that they would prefer materials developed in their own region.
     In summary, the results from the dialect mapping sessions indicate that, despite some linguistic
differences, Kurux speakers in India and Nepal have a unified identity. Despite some differences
across Nepal and northern Bihar, speakers report high comprehension of the Kurux spoken in these
areas. There was no consensus between dialect mapping sessions on how well Kurux speakers in
Nepal can understand speakers from other areas in India, such as Jharkhand and West Bengal, but it
is clear they perceive more linguistic difference from those areas than within Nepali Kurux (and
nearby Bihar). Likewise, no one variety was agreed upon by all as the best for language development.
6    Language development considerations

One goal of this study was to assess the desires of Kurux speakers in Nepal to develop their language
and to explore the possibility of using existing materials from Jharkhand, India. Through
orthography testing, interviews, and observations, it was discovered that the existing Devanagari
Kurux orthography from India would be suitable for use in Nepal, with some awareness-raising and
training. However, the existing materials from Jharkhand may be difficult for Nepali Kurux to
understand, as the language variety there is notably different from the language in Nepal. Despite
these potential difficulties, Kurux speakers in Nepal expressed a desire to access more books and
other materials from Jharkhand. Many also expressed excitement about the possibility of reading and
writing in their language, and some already do so. Positive language attitudes and high language
vitality suggest that the Kurux community would be a good candidate for activities such as literacy
classes, orthography fluency workshops, and multilingual education (MLE).
6.1     Orthography suitability
Many language development practitioners have commented on the importance of assessing
adaptation potential and the various factors that should be considered in this type of assessment.
Clare O’Leary states that “those involved in a language program should put every effort into
discovering whether [standardization or extending existing materials] is feasible before embarking
on a separate program” (1994:13). Joseph Grimes notes that “many things get translated widely in
today’s world: technical manuals, diplomatic documents, news, religious books, reference works,
sales pitches, literature, textbooks, business dispatches, scientific communications, and on and on”
(1992:27). He goes on to list compatibility of cultures, semantics and pragmatics, syntax and
discourse structure, and morphological distinctions as being important factors in adaptation of
written text from one language to another.

27

    Orthography testing was used in this study to assess the existing Devanagari orthography used
by Kurux speakers in India with regard to its suitability for Kurux speakers in Nepal.23 Because
linguistic similarity between the Kurux varieties under question was proposed to be high, this simple
orthography test was meant to give a preliminary view of the suitability of existing written materials
from India for Kurux speakers in Nepal. The test consisted of a short piece of text approximately 120
words long, taken from a book published in modified Devanagari script in Jharkhand, which
speakers were asked to read aloud. Speakers were then evaluated on the ease with which they were
able to read the text and were asked their opinions of the language and orthography. (See Appendix
D for the full text and detailed methodology.) Rather than eliminating unsuitable subjects through
the use of a pre-test in Nepali, only Kurux speakers who had completed class 10 were invited to read
the text. This criterion meant that a disproportionate number of test subjects were young and male,
leaving little room for stratification of results. Despite this, the researchers are confident the final
sample of 23 individuals was sufficiently representative of the population to give an adequate
understanding of the suitability of the existing orthography for use in Nepal.
    Most respondents had difficulty reading the story aloud, although some improved as they
worked through the text. Most had never read in their own language before, many people seemed
nervous, and one was unable to finish reading the story. When asked to retell the main points of the
text, only one person was able to recall more than half of the expected points, and two gave no
response. These results may be an indication that the orthography and/or language were difficult for
respondents, but it could also be a result of difficulty with reading aloud, with the type of text, or
with unfamiliarity with summarizing text.
     After reading the text, respondents were asked how difficult they found the orthography. Half
expressed that it was difficult to read, while the other half said it was “a little difficult” or “okay.”
Interestingly, there was no correlation between how difficult people found the script and how much
of the story they were able to recall. When asked further about the orthography, approximately a
third of participants mentioned it was difficult because they had never read it before, but with
practice it would get easier. Two people mentioned difficulties with “pronunciation,” which likely
refers to sounds in the Kurux language which have no equivalent in Devanagari script.24
    Respondents were also asked how well they understood the story and how different they
thought the words in the text were from their own way of speaking. Perceived understanding varied:
two-thirds of people reported understanding most or all (35% and 30% respectively) of the story, a
quarter felt they only understood half, and the rest only understood a little. A third of respondents
mentioned that their difficulties were caused by the fact that some of the words in the story were
different from their own. A few commented that the language in the text was old fashioned,
consistent with other reports that the language in Jharkhand is more similar to how older people in
Nepal speak Kurux. One man, who enjoyed the story, said it contained “words like I haven’t heard in
20 years.”
   When asked directly about the vocabulary in the story, most said it was different or a little
different (30% and 35%), but a few (17%) said the words were the same, and another 17 percent
stated they were very different. Readers considered the text to be their own language, but most
guessed it was written in a place that speaks a different variety from theirs.
     Despite the difficulties Kurux speakers had with reading the text and despite the recognized
differences from their own varieties, orthography test respondents were interested in and excited
about reading a text in their own language. All but one person said they would like to read more
Kurux texts.25
     In summary, Kurux speakers in Nepal overall found the text difficult to read, but it appears that
most of the difficulty comes from lack of exposure and reading fluency. However, many people did
also mention that some of the words in the book were unfamiliar to them, meaning that beyond the
orthography the difference in dialect is a challenge to extensibility of existing literature from
Jharkhand. Despite these difficulties, a majority of participants expressed that they understood most

6.2      Desires for language development
Along with the positive language attitudes Kurux speakers expressed towards their own language (see
section 4.3), the great majority of people we talked to were interested in the possibility of reading
and writing in their language. When asked if they saw an advantage to reading and writing in Kurux,
78 percent of interview respondents said “yes” and most were enthusiastic in their responses. Many
expressed it would be easier to learn to read and write in their own language. Several people
mentioned that reading and writing would help maintain their unique language and culture, and still
others commented that having a writing system would help them teach others about their language
and culture. Several mentioned that having a writing system would aid in teaching children and
general development.
    Of those who perceived no advantage to reading and writing in Kurux, a few thought that there
would be no advantage because other people couldn’t read it. Others mentioned that learning the
orthography might be difficult or that they were illiterate, so it would be of no benefit to them. A
few expressed that most Kurux speakers can read and write in Nepali, and that Nepali is more
advantageous than the mother tongue.
   When asked specifically what kinds of Kurux materials people would be interested in, about half
of interview respondents mentioned books, and about a quarter mentioned news/radio programs.
One man said he had seen books and songs from India and expressed a wish that more of these
materials were available in Nepal.
    While there are desires for literacy and materials in Kurux, few people in Nepal are aware of an
existing orthography or materials in their language. Despite this, 26 percent of interview respondents
said that people in their village write in Kurux, mostly for informal communication and likely with
improvised Devanagari spellings. Several people mentioned using Kurux when texting with friends,
on Facebook, writing letters, and writing lists. A couple of people mentioned the Kurux section of the
Gorkha Patra magazine, which publishes writings in various languages of Nepal, but they also said
that finding copies of the magazine can be difficult. One man we met has been gathering songs and
poems for a Kurux book, which he hopes to publish soon. These intentional efforts to write in the
Kurux language show a movement in the community towards literacy in the mother tongue. There is
also support from the Nepal Oraon Indigenous Foundation for literacy in Kurux; they have hosted
various programs to support the development of the Kurux language in Nepal.
    Data gathered during this study indicate that the Kurux community in Nepal would be a good
candidate for literacy classes in the local language. Literacy levels throughout the community are
low, with 56 percent of interview respondents having little or no education. However, as shown in
table 12, some in the community are highly educated, and more and more younger people are
completing SLC26 and beyond.
