     In summary, Kurux speakers in Nepal are interested in materials in their own language, and
most see an advantage to reading and writing in Kurux. Some people in Nepal use Devanagari script
to write in Kurux, but very few people are aware of existing Kurux materials from Jharkhand. The
strong interest in reading and writing in Kurux, along with signs of community initiative with regard
to developing their language and a relatively strong language vitality, would make the Kurux
community a good candidate for literacy programs and MLE.
7    Language vitality

The language vitality in the Kurux community in Nepal27 is strong but shows some signs of erosion.
In some areas, the language is being maintained well and should be considered EGIDS level 6a:
Sustainable Orality, and, although there are signs of deteriorating vitality in other areas, as a whole,
the Kurux language in Nepal is EGIDS level 6a: Vigorous.28 (See Appendix H for more on the EGIDS
and the Sustainable Use Model.)
     In many areas, there is widespread use of the language, but even in these areas, Kurux use could
erode due to lack of strong differentiation, or clear social rules guiding languages choice. Language
attitudes among Kurux speakers are generally positive, ethnolinguistic identity is strong, and
situational factors create sufficient motivation for continued use of the language. Additionally, in
many areas, children are acquiring the language at a young age and continuing to use it as they grow
older, although in some places children are abandoning Kurux in favor of Nepali. The Kurux
community would benefit from activities that increase their awareness of strategies for maintaining
language vitality, in order to arrest erosion of language vitality in their communities.
    The main tools used in assessing language vitality in this study were interviews and observation.
A total of 50 people in Nepal were interviewed (excluding Tokla, where the vitality situation is very
different and will be discussed separately). Of the interviewees, 27 were female and 23 male, and 22
illiterate and 28 literate. There were sufficient interview responses to allow for three age brackets,
and so for questions relating to vitality those aged 15 to 25 are considered ‘young’, those 26 to40 are
considered ‘middle-aged’, and those 41 and older are considered ‘old.’
    For this study, the vitality of the Kurux language in Nepal was assessed using concepts from the
Sustainable Use Model developed by Lewis and Simons (2016). From the FAMED conditions, the
following questions were addressed: Is the language sufficient for the desired functions, and is there
differentiation between languages? Are there sufficient internal motivations to use the language, and
minimal or no external opposition to the language? Are there sufficient methods for children to learn
the language? (See Appendix H for more about EGIDS and the FAMED conditions.)

7.1      Patterns of language use
The Uranw people of Nepal primarily reside in the southern tropical plains, an area known as the
Terai. This area of the country is known for its high diversity of languages, with people of different
ethnic groups and languages living in close proximity. Despite living in these highly multilingual
areas, most Uranw people have maintained their Kurux language and culture.
    For interviews and tools in this study, the sample is a highly multilingual group, with men
speaking an average of 4.2 languages, and women an average of 3.5 languages, and similar levels of
multilingualism across generations. Nearly every respondent reported that Kurux was their best
language,29 and the common second-best languages were Nepali (56%), Bhojpuri (15%), and Maithili
(5%). In Bhokraha (Sunsari), the majority of people speak Nepali second best, but Maithili is also
common. Most respondents from Lochani (Morang) speak Nepali second best, while in Siddhapur
(Parsa), Bhojpuri30 is the most common second language, followed by Nepali. Across all sites,
significantly more young people speak Nepali second best (79%) than middle-aged (54%) and older
people (31%). The level of proficiency in Nepali also correlates with the levels of education.
Multilingualism is not decreasing across generations, but there is a clear shift away from proficiency
in other local languages towards proficiency in Nepali.
     Despite being highly multilingual, the majority of Kurux speakers report using their own
language with their own people most of the time, showing patterns of differentiation and defying the
general trend in Nepal. Of the 50 individual interview respondents, 84 percent reported that they
never use other languages with other Kurux people. Lochani had the highest reported use of Nepali
with other Kurux people compared to Bhokraha and Siddhapur (see table 13). These reports were
confirmed by observation in Lochani of some Kurux men using Nepali with other Kurux speakers.

                          Siddhapur      94%      6%
                            Overall average  84%      16%
    As was also confirmed by observation, more men than women reported using Nepali with other
Kurux people. One young woman told us that her mother scolds her if she does not speak Kurux,
saying, “What? Do we speak Nepali now?” Age is also a predictive factor; all older people said they
use only Kurux in the village, compared to 76 percent of the middle-aged and 79 percent of young
people. The fact that similar numbers of the young and middle-aged people report exclusive use of
Kurux in the village is an encouraging sign that language use has not significantly deteriorated in
recent years.
    Language use among children shows a similar pattern to that of adults; 80 percent of interview
respondents said children exclusively use Kurux when playing with other children. Again, rates were
significantly lower in Lochani, with 65 percent reporting exclusive use of Kurux among children. In
Bhokraha, 100 percent of respondents stated that children use Kurux with each other. One man said
children from other ethnic groups learn Kurux when the children of the village play together. In
Siddhapur, nearly everyone reported that children use at least some Kurux, and 77 percent said they
exclusively use Kurux. One respondent mentioned that children there use Nepali if children from
other ethnic groups are present, showing some differentiation.
    Use of the Kurux language in the home is also high. It is quite unusual for anything but Kurux to
be used with spouses, parents, and children.31 Of interview respondents who were married, all but
four said they use only Kurux in the home, and only one reported speaking Nepali exclusively with
his spouse. All interview respondents said they use Kurux with older people, and the vast majority

said they use only Kurux with children as well. These trends were generally confirmed by
observation, although in Lochani some Kurux men were heard using Nepali with children.
    Another important factor in assessing language vitality is differentiation, meaning clear social
rules dictating when to use the language. Differentiation allows communities to maintain stable
multilingualism. These rules and trends can be difficult for outsiders to observe, especially since the
speakers themselves may not be able to articulate what guides their language choices in different
situations. A few Kurux speakers mentioned that they use other languages only when non-Kurux
people are present, or that they use only Nepali at school or when helping children with schoolwork.
Despite observing few signs of intentional differentiation, the language-use patterns at present do
show encouraging signs of differentiation supporting language maintenance.
    The Kurux-speaking community in Nepal may still benefit from raised awareness of the value of
differentiation. It is especially important for people who speak languages with high vitality to
address the issue of differentiation, as they often assume that their language will continue being
spoken naturally when in reality other languages such as Nepali will begin to be used in more and
more domains of life.
     In summary, Kurux use is high in these villages across all demographic groups and all domains,
and there is some evidence of differentiation. While Kurux use is decreasing somewhat, younger
people do not use the language significantly less than middle-aged people, and most children are
using Kurux frequently, all signs that language vitality is strong.
7.2     Contextual factors motivating language use
Patterns of language use are not the only factors that influence the vitality of a language. In order for
a language to be used regularly by a community, there must be motivations to choose to speak that
language rather than another. The Uranw community has a strong sense of identity, and an integral
part of that identity is the Kurux language. There are many contextual factors that encourage
continued use of the Kurux language, both inside speech communities and external to them.
     Despite living in villages made up of many ethnicities and languages, as discussed in section 7.1,
all of the groups under study live in neighborhoods that are almost exclusively Kurux. So, even
though Kurux people have frequent, even daily, interactions with people who speak other languages,
the homogeneity of their communities means they maintain relationships with people who prefer to
speak Kurux. Intermarriage is almost nonexistent in these communities. Both parents of every
interview respondent were Uranw and spoke Kurux with them as children. In addition, nearly every
interview respondent’s parents were local to that village or grew up nearby. In Nepal, mixed-
language marriages are a common reason to shift away from using the mother tongue, but in Kurux
communities this is not an influencing factor.
    Another common motivation to shift away from use of the mother tongue is for access to
economic and educational opportunities, but this is not a factor threatening language use for Kurux
speakers in Nepal. The fact that these Kurux communities are located in the Terai means they have
access to larger towns and cities; the most remote area we visited was Siddhapur, which was only an
hour’s drive from a larger population center and two hours from the city of Birganj. All the Kurux
villages under study are primarily farming communities, but there is ample opportunity for other
types of occupations such as teaching, office work, business ownership, and technical jobs. Many
Kurux people, especially of younger generations, have left their home areas for higher education or
work, but most return frequently for visits or permanently resettle in Kurux areas.
     Likewise, educational opportunities are ample, and it was reported most children attend primary
school, all in local schools. Those who do attend secondary school typically do so locally, and some
Kurux areas are close enough to universities that it is possible to live in the village while getting a
higher education. It was reported that even though Nepali is the only language used in the classroom
at all levels, children typically use Kurux or a mix of Kurux and other languages with each other at
school. Even for those who use Nepali at school, the fact that they spend their time in a Kurux village
outside of school hours means there are social and cultural motivations to continue using Kurux.
    Most Kurux speakers have strong desires for their language to be passed on to future
generations. In individual interviews, respondents were asked which language they thought was best
for children to learn first. The vast majority (88%) stated it was important for children to learn Kurux
first. Those who said Nepali should be taught in the home expressed it would improve educational
opportunities. All who preferred Nepali for their children’s first language were uneducated women

32

who likely had experienced difficulties in their life because of low proficiency in Nepali. Some also
mentioned the need for children to learn multiple languages well, such as one teacher who is
teaching his young children both Kurux and Nepali so they will maintain their own culture and also
do well in school. Another man emphatically stated, “Because of development, you need to speak
English and Nepali, but you should not forget your own language!”
    Outside influences, such as government policy or other groups’ perceptions of the language, can
be a motivating factor in patterns of language use. Data gathered for this study indicate that while
outsiders do not have negative attitudes towards Kurux, it is not seen as especially prestigious by
outsiders. It is not common for outsiders to learn the language; “We speak everyone else’s
languages,” one Kurux man in Parsa told us. A few people did report that children from other groups
learn a little Kurux, and that kids are not ashamed to use the language in front of their classmates.
These neutral attitudes by outsiders mean that external factors do not discourage Kurux people from
speaking their language.
    Government policy can sometimes negatively affect language vitality. This is not the case in
Nepal, as the Constitution of Nepal affirms all languages spoken in Nepal as languages of the nation,
calling for the Language Commission to “protect and develop” these many languages. In addition, the
Constitution states that “every Nepalese community residing in Nepal shall have the right to get
education in its mother tongue and, for that purpose, to open and operate schools and educational
institutes, in accordance with law” (Federal Democratic Republic of Nepal 2016).
    The context in which these Kurux communities exist encourage continued use of the Kurux
language. The living situation, social environment, and government policy supports continued use of
the Kurux language, and most people desire to see it passed on to future generations.
7.3     Language acquisition
Language acquisition by children is often assumed to be the only factor determining the vitality of a
language. While this undue focus is misplaced, sufficient methods of acquisition are required for a
language to maintain stable vitality. In the Kurux communities visited for this study, there is ample
opportunity for children to learn their mother tongue.
     Children in the Kurux community in Nepal learn the Kurux language from a young age. In
Bhokraha and Siddhapur, all interview respondents said children in their village exclusively speak
Kurux until they start school, and only then do they begin to learn Nepali. In Lochani, children learn
Nepali earlier, but still learn Kurux from their parents and others. Because children all attend school
locally, they are able to continue gaining proficiency in Kurux as they get older by using the
language with their family and friends.
     Intermarriage is extremely uncommon in these communities; all respondents came from families
where both parents spoke Kurux. Nearly all adults, regardless of age, reported that they use Kurux or
a mixture of Kurux and Nepali with children. We observed most parents speaking Kurux with their
children, although in some areas children were observed using Nepali with each other.
    Of interviewees who had children, 96 percent said that their children speak Kurux well or very
well. Only two people mentioned that some of their children do not speak Kurux well, and said it
was because they have left the area and are forgetting the language. A few people gave reports of
young people mixing the language with other languages or speaking Kurux less than adults. Most,
however, thought young people speak the language well. One man stated, “In our group, [we teach]
our own language first.”
    Not every Kurux-speaking area has such universal acquisition. In Lochani, there were a few
young people who were not very confident in the language and preferred to use Nepali. We observed
some fathers using Nepali with their children. There were also reports of other Kurux areas where
children are no longer learning the language.
    The homogenous nature of neighborhoods in these villages and the low level of intermarriage
creates a positive environment for children to acquire their mother tongue at an early age. The
proximity of primary schools also allows for children to live at home, allowing them to continue
using the language with their families once they start school. It also means that, in some schools, the
children practice the language with each other while at school as well. Most people reported that
young people speak the language well, but some said that younger people mix Kurux with other
languages, indicating a possible shift away from the mother tongue in younger generations. There

33

were also reports of areas, especially in larger population centers and near major roads, where
children no longer speak the Kurux language.
7.4     Language vitality in Tokla, Jhapa
The Kurux community in Jhapa is unique within Nepal, and therefore will be addressed separately
here. The Tokla Tea Farm and surrounding area is a migrant community, and the Kurux people who
live there migrated from Jharkhand and West Bengal thirty to forty years ago. Only those who were
born in India speak Kurux, and the language appears to have low prestige. The ethnically Kurux
community maintains a unique identity distinct from the myriad of other groups in the area; this
identity is not defined by the Kurux language. Young people do not identify themselves with the
Kurux language. One young man told us, “If they ask us in school what our mother tongue is, we say
Nepali because we do not speak Kurux.”
    One reason for this language shift to Nepali and Sadri32 is the mixed nature of the area.
Everyone works in the tea fields all day, interacting with people who speak Nepali, Tamang, Limbu,
Rai, and other languages. When asked why he prefers to use Nepali, one man said, “We spend eight
hours a day at school with our friends [of mixed caste] and only three in the home. Of course we
speak Nepali!”
8    Summary and recommendations

8.1    Summary of findings
This report presents the findings of research on the Kurux (Uranw) language community in Nepal
with a focus on their relationship to the Kurux language community in India. The purpose of the
research was accomplished by gathering data on linguistic variation between Nepal and India,
determining levels of comprehension of the Kurux spoken in India among Nepali Kurux speakers,
seeking to understand the desires for language development and extensibility of existing Indian
Kurux materials, and assessing the language vitality and ethnolinguistic attitudes of Uranw people in
Nepal.
    The Kurux people of South Asia originated in the Chota Nagpur plateau in India, and in the past
few centuries, some Kurux speakers have migrated to other areas of India, Bangladesh, Bhutan, and
Nepal. Multiple names have been used to refer to the Kurux language and its people. ‘Kurux’ is
typically used to refer to the language and is the autoglottonym for the language and people. ‘Oraon’
or ‘Uranw’ is commonly used for the ethnic group and is the officially accepted term in India and
Nepal, but ‘Kurux’ is also an acceptable term for the people. ‘Dhangar’ and ‘Jhangar’ are outdated
terms that were assigned to the language and community by outsiders and are not accepted by the
Kurux community.
    The research regarding ethnolinguistic identity indicated that Kurux speakers in Nepal and India
see themselves as being one united group, despite low levels of contact between them. Kurux
speakers in Nepal have positive attitudes toward all varieties of their language, and most had
enthusiastically positive attitudes towards actual samples of speech from Jharkhand and West
Bengal, further supporting that these groups have a unified ethnolinguistic identity.
     Linguistic analysis revealed that the lexical similarity between varieties in Nepal is high, ranging
from 84 to 92 percent. The lexical similarity between Kurux in Nepal and India is lower, but not
drastically so. This comparison showed the lexical similarity to the variety from Jharkhand ranging
from 71 to 89 percent and ranging from 74 to 83 percent to the variety in West Bengal. Intelligibility
testing of the Jharkhand variety in Nepal resulted in an overall score of 86 percent with a standard
deviation of 11 percent. This result, in conjunction with positive attitudes towards the speech in the
Jharkhand story, support the conclusion that comprehension of the Kurux from Jharkhand is high
and that speakers in Nepal perceive it to be their own language. The West Bengal speech variety also
received positive reactions. Perceived comprehension of the story from West Bengal was similarly
high, and although it was also seen as part of the Kurux language, speakers in Nepal perceived it to
be somewhat different from the speech in Jharkhand.
32 Sadri is a common language of wider communication in Jhapa and is commonly used to communicate in the
tea fields.

34

    The conclusion that comprehension is high between different varieties and that speakers
consider the varieties in Nepal and India to be one unified language, is also evident in results from
dialect mapping and interviews. Kurux people in Nepal include all varieties of Kurux in their
ethnolinguistic group, despite recognizing some linguistic variation within Nepal and northern Bihar,
and reporting that some varieties in Jharkhand, West Bengal, and other parts of India are somewhat
difficult to understand.
    Kurux speakers in Nepal express interest in reading and writing in their language, and some
already do so. Positive language attitudes and high language vitality in most Kurux-speaking areas
suggest that the Kurux community of Nepal would be a good candidate for activities such as literacy
classes, orthography fluency workshops, and multilingual education (MLE).
    With regard to the possibility of using existing Kurux literature and materials from Jharkhand,
orthography testing and interviews revealed that the existing Devanagari Kurux orthography would
be suitable for use in Nepal. However, existing materials from India may be difficult for Nepali
speakers to understand, as the written language variety has some notable differences from the
language spoken in Nepal. Despite these challenges, Kurux speakers in Nepal expressed desires to
access more books and other materials from India.
    The current overall level of Kurux vitality in Nepal is 6a on the EGIDS, indicating that language
use is strong in most communities and will likely continue to be maintained in future generations.
The language is seen as useful for all domains. There is ample opportunity to use the language, and
there are strong motivating factors supporting continued use of Kurux in most communities.
     In conclusion, the Kurux spoken in Nepal is one language with that of the Kurux spoken in
India. Nepali Kurux speakers have high comprehension of Indian Kurux, and there is potential for the
two groups to share materials. However, there are enough linguistic differences that speakers in
Nepal would also benefit from materials developed in their own varieties.
8.2     Recommendations
Based on the conclusions of this research, the following recommendations are given concerning
future language development in the Kurux language community in Nepal.
      First, the ISO code [kxl] for Kurux in Nepal should be retired, and the Kurux language of Nepal
should be included under the international Kurux ISO code [kru].
    Second, activities should be undertaken in the Kurux community of Nepal to raise awareness of
existing Indian Kurux materials and the existing Kurux Devanagari orthography. Although the
language in India differs from that of Nepal, Nepali Kurux speakers desire increased access to existing
Kurux literature and other materials. Beneficial activities may include orthography promotion
workshops, literacy workshops, and Kurux materials distribution.
     Third, Kurux language materials should be developed (or adapted) specifically for Nepali Kurux.
Standardization of written Nepali Kurux would make materials more easily understood by all
speakers in Nepal. Beneficial activities may include writing workshops; compilation of Kurux poems,
songs, and stories; and story and song recording.
     Fourth, multilingual education (MLE) materials should be developed in the Kurux language in
Nepal. Kurux communities in Nepal with high language vitality would be good candidates for Kurux
language preschool and primary school programs. The Kurux community would benefit from
collaboration with experts in MLE, especially those who have already taken initiative to start these
types of programs in their local communities.
     Fifth, awareness-raising activities for language preservation should be undertaken by the Kurux
community. Although some Kurux communities in Nepal have strong language vitality, there are
some signs of erosion which could cause language shift. Understanding of the factors that aid in
language maintenance and continued use of the language into future generations would allow the
Kurux community to strengthen their language and encourage continued use of the Kurux language
in future generations.

B.2      Lexical similarity comparison procedures
For a lexical similarity count, the wordlists are compared in order to determine the extent to which
the vocabulary of each pair of speech forms is similar. No attempt is made to identify genuine
cognates based on a network of sound correspondences. Rather, two lexical items are judged to be
phonetically similar if at least half of the segments compared are the same (category 1) and of the
remaining segments at least half are rather similar (category 2). For example, if two items of eight
segments in length are compared, these words are judged to be similar if at least four segments are
virtually the same and at least two are rather similar. The criteria applied are:
    Category 1
        ••Consonants (consonant-like) segments which match exactly          Vowels (vowel-like) segments which match exactly or differ by only one  articulatory
 •feature           Phonetically similar consonant segments (of the sort which frequently are found  as
           allophones, often differing in only one articulatory feature) which are seen to correspond
 Categoryin at2 least three pairs of words
        •  All other phonetically similar pairs of segments which are not supported by at least three
            pairs of words
        •  Vowels which differ by two or more articulatory features
    Category 3
••  Pairs of segments which are not phonetically similar       A segment which is matched by no segment in the corresponding item and position 
    Other criteria used specifically for the analysis of this survey data are:
        •  In the case of metathesis and reduplication, words are considered similar.
        •  Breathy consonants are considered category 1 with aspirated consonants (e.g., [b̤] and
             [bʰ]). These are allophones of each other (Gordon 1976).
        •  Fricatives and affricates in a similar place of articulation are considered category 2 (e.g.,
            [s] and [tʃ]).
        •   [χ] and [kʰ] are considered category 2.
        •  Retroflex consonants [ʈ] and [ɖ] are considered category 2 with retroflex flaps [ɽ].
        •  The schwa vowel [ə] is considered category 1 with [ʌ], [ɔ], and [ɑ].
        •   [ɾ], [ɽ], and [ɹ] are considered category 1 because their place of articulation is affected by
            their environment (Gordon 1976). The trills [r] and [ɽ͡r] are considered category 2 with
           these segments.
        •  In some conditions, nasal vowels are treated as similar to a vowel followed by a nasal
           stop (e.g., [ã] and [an]).
        •  Retroflex nasals before retroflex stops are considered category 1 with non-retroflex nasals
              (e.g., [ɳɖ] and [nd]).
        •  The inter-consonantal schwa vowel [ə], which Gordon calls the “relic vowel” is caused by
            partial deletion over time, a “systematic reduction of what at some stage was a fully
            syllabic vowel” (1976:65). For analysis, the “relic vowel” is typically ignored, as per
             Blair’s recommendations for analyzing South Asian languages (1990:32).
        •  “Glottal catch” acts as an approximant, separating morphemes. In most environments, it
              is treated as a unit phoneme.

    The analysis was done using Cog software,34 with manual adjustments. Cog compares varieties
in a pairwise fashion using an iterative approach. In the comparison, the following tasks are
automatically performed for each variety pair:
        •  Align and compute a phonetic similarity for each word pair
        •  Identify regular sound correspondences
        •  Identify likely cognates
    Cog aligns word pairs by computing a phonetic distance for each segment pair using a built-in
knowledge of IPA. This information is used to compute a numerical value that represents the
phonetic similarity of a pair of words. Once sound correspondences have been identified, Cog will
adjust the alignment and phonetic similarity of lexical items in an iterative fashion. If a
correspondence is very regular, the phonetic distance is reduced between the corresponding
segments. Cog can then use these correspondences to identify likely cognates, creating a foundation
for calculating lexical similarity percentages.
    The basic settings used in Cog were as follows:
        •  Alignment mode: Full (global)
        •  Automatic syllabification: Enabled (Combine consonants in same syllable position, do not
         combine vowels in the same syllable position)
        •   Initial cognate threshold: 30 percent
        •  Method: Blair
        •  Default regular correspondence threshold: 3 (Automatically determine if possible)
        •  Ignore regular insertions/deletions
        •  Regular consonant correspondences are treated as category 1
        •  Similar vowel distance threshold: 600
        •  Similar consonant distance threshold: 600

Appendix C: Recorded Text Tests
The extent to which speakers of related linguistic varieties understand one another can be studied by
means of recorded texts. Such studies investigate whether speakers of one variety understand a
narrative text of another variety and are able to answer questions about the content of that text. The
accuracy with which subjects answer these questions is taken as an indicator of their comprehension
of that speech form. From the percentage of correct answers, the amount of intelligibility between
speech forms is inferred. The recorded text testing used in this survey is based on the procedures
described in Casad (1974) and Blair (1990).
     Short, personal-experience narratives are deemed to be most suitable for recorded text testing in
that the content must be relatively unpredictable and the speech form should be natural. Folklore or
other material that is widely known is avoided. A three-to-five-minute story is recorded from a
speaker of the regional vernacular. The story is then transcribed and a set of comprehension
questions is constructed based on various semantic domains covered in the text. A set of twenty to
twenty-five questions is initially prepared and then checked with speakers from the same region to
ensure that the spoken forms are truly representative of that area (this is known as a Hometown Test
or HTT). Some of the questions will prove unsuitable because the answer is not clear in the text or
because the question is confusing to native speakers of the test variety. Unsuitable questions are then
deleted from the preliminary set, leaving a minimum of ten final questions for each recorded text test
(RTT).
    The HTT helps to ensure that native speakers of the text dialect could accurately answer the
comprehension questions. Once a text has been hometown tested with a minimum of ten subjects
who have been able to correctly answer the selected comprehension questions, averaging scores of
90 percent or above, the test is considered validated.
     Before administering the RTT in each location, the selected questions must be recorded in the
regional variety of the test subjects. This ensures that measures of comprehension are based on the
subjects’ understanding of the text itself and not on a misunderstanding of the test questions.
     In the RTTs, test subjects hear the complete story once, after which the story is repeated with
test questions and opportunities for responses interspersed with necessary pauses in the recorded
text. Appropriate and correct responses are directly extractable from the segment of speech
immediately preceding the question. Thus the RTT aims to be a close reflection of a subject’s
comprehension of the language itself, not of their memory, intelligence, or reasoning. The average or
mean of the scores obtained from subjects at one test location is taken as a numerical indicator of the
intelligibility between speakers of the dialect represented.
      It is possible that a subject may be unable to answer the test questions correctly because they do
not understand what is expected. This is especially true with uneducated subjects or those
unacquainted with test-taking. Therefore, a short pre-test story with ten questions is recorded in the
local variety before beginning the actual testing. The purpose of the pre-test is to teach the subject
what is expected according to the RTT procedures. If the subject is able to answer the pre-test
questions, it is assumed that they would serve as a suitable subject for the RTT. Occasionally, a
subject fails to perform adequately on the pre-test. Performances of such subjects are eliminated from
the final evaluation, the assumption being that uncontrollable factors unrelated to the intelligibility
of speech forms are skewing the test results. Generally, subjects performing at levels of less than 70
percent on the pre-test are eliminated from further testing.
    There are many factors that may affect the variation of scores within one test site. Contact with
the variety being tested is one such factor, among many others. For this reason, it is important to
include a measure of dispersion which reflects the extent to which the range of scores varies from the
mean: the Standard Deviation. On an RTT with 100 possible points (100 percent), standard
deviations of more than 12 to 15 are considered high. If the standard deviation is relatively low (10–
12 or below) and the mean score for the subjects from the selected test point is high, the implication
is that the community as a whole probably understands the test variety rather well. If the standard
deviation is low and the mean RTT score is also low, the implication is that the community as a
whole understands the test variety rather poorly and that regular contact has not facilitated learning
of the test variety to any significant extent. If the standard deviation is high, regardless of the mean
score, one implication is that some subjects comprehend the test variety better than others. In this
last case, inherent intelligibility between the related varieties may be mixed with acquired

    High standard deviations can result from many causes, such as inconsistencies in the
circumstances of test administration and scoring or differences in attentiveness of subjects.
Researchers involved in recorded text testing need to be aware of the potential for skewed results
due to such factors and to control for them as much as possible through careful test development and
administration.
     In contrast to experimentally controlled testing in a laboratory or classroom situation, the
results of field-administered methods such as the RTT cannot be completely isolated from potential
biases. Recorded texts and test questions will vary in terms of the clarity of the recording.
Comparisons of RTT results from different texts need to be made cautiously. It is therefore
recommended that results from RTTs not be interpreted in terms of fixed numerical thresholds, but
rather evaluated in light of other indicators of intelligibility such as lexical similarity, dialect
opinions, and reported patterns of contact and communication. In general, however, RTT mean
scores of around 80 percent or higher with accompanying low standard deviations are usually taken
to indicate that representatives of the test point dialect display adequate understanding of the variety
represented by the recording. Conversely, RTT means below 60 percent are interpreted to indicate
inadequate intelligibility.
    Responses to questions asked after the administration of an RTT can reflect attitudes held
toward the test dialect. These opinions can also help the researcher interpret the scores obtained on
the tests.
     All storytellers and participants involved in the recorded text testing gave oral and recorded
informed consent before assisting with this research.

D.2     Orthography test text
The following text was excerpted from a Kurux book from Jharkhand, short stories by Fransiska
Kujur, (फ्राłȫसʀका कुजुर) (Kujur 2011:42). A paragraph was selected that had a relatively contained
narrative, and that took about 1.5–2 minutes to read aloud.
Kurux text





English translation
Having heard the name “Karma” from Vinita, the old woman looked at the face of Vinita and said,
“You are the daughter of Mrs. Sukro! No! Oh, because of my poor eyesight I could not recognize you.
You are away from home so how would you know the situation in my family? Chhandu (my son) is
of your age, no, but he has spoiled his life. He sold our agricultural land and bought a car, but the
car is just [sitting] in front of our house. He was drunk and he was driving the car and [got in] an
accident and it got very damaged and is just [sitting] at home. Again he sold some of our agricultural
land and [is] constructing a building. One day he had a quarrel with his wife and he chased her
away. And now he is living with a woman who is from a blacksmith family without marriage. How
could I adjust with them? So I came out from my home and I am begging here. How can I live a
polluted life before I die? What shall I do? I am living just alone.”

Appendix G: Dialect Mapping
G.1      Dialect mapping procedures
Dialect mapping is a participatory methods tool. Participatory methods tools are ideally led by a
trained facilitator and facilitated with the interaction of both men and women of various ages and
educational backgrounds from the language community. The facilitator poses questions to the
community and requests answers to be written on slips of paper (one answer per paper). These
papers are then arranged by the community in various ways requested by the facilitator.
    The purpose of this tool is to assist speakers of a specific dialect in discussing information they
already know about the dialects and levels of comprehension between dialects. Another purpose is to
encourage them to think about which varieties of their language could use a single set of written or
oral materials.
    The steps for facilitating dialect mapping are provided here in English, but facilitation was done
in Nepali. The steps were modified as deemed necessary by the researcher at the time of the
facilitation.
     1. What is the name of your language? (If there is more than one name for the language, ask
       which name they prefer.)
     2. Where are the major locations where your language is spoken?
     3. Place these papers on the ground to show which places are next to each other. (Use north,
        south, east, and west to create a map on the ground.)
     4. What other languages are so similar to your language that when they speak, you can
       understand at least some words? Write the names of these languages on pieces of paper and
       add them to the “map” on the ground.
     5. Do the people in any of these places speak your language in the same way? If so, place a
        small loop of string around each such group.
     6. Which variety do you understand best? Second best? Place the appropriate number next to
       each group.
     7. Which of these varieties do you understand completely? Which do you understand most?
      Which do you understand about half? And which do you only understand a little? In which
        of these villages can you understand the way they speak completely? Using the key showing
        faces that represent different levels of understanding, please indicate your level of
       comprehension of each variety.
     8. When you speak to people from these other places, do you each speak your own variety? Or
      do you use your own variety and they also use your variety? Or do you use their variety? Or
      do you each use another variety for easier understanding? Using the key showing colors that
        represent different ways of speaking, please indicate how you speak with others.
     9.  If books, films, pamphlets, or other materials were developed in your language, which place
       would be the best for development so that all the other places could use the materials?
      Which place would be second best? Place the appropriate Nepali letter next to each choice to
       rank where you think is best.

    EGIDS Level 5 (Developing)
        •  This is the level at which literacy is incipient, more often than not through informal
           educational structures and systems and with only weak or transient societal institutional
           support as defined above.
        •  Although the introduction of literacy can serve powerfully to improve the prestige of a
           minority language and may increase its prospects for survival in many cases, the stronger
            institutional support for literacy acquisition and maintenance found at the EGIDS level 4
              is required for ongoing transmission of local-language literacy from one generation to the
            next. The presence of incipient literacy in a speech community is not in itself sufficient to
          ensure sustainable ongoing use of the language.

                                      123

124

        •  Furthermore, the existence of an orthography or the production of some literature are
            not, in themselves, sufficient to qualify a language as having achieved EGIDS level 5.
          Reading and writing must actually be used by some segment, albeit a small one, of the
            overall population. Many communities where preparations for the introduction of literacy
          have been initiated are effectively at EGIDS 6a (Vigorous). To qualify as EGIDS level 5,
           the language must also be in vigorous use as described for level 6a; when the language is
           losing uses and users, it should not be classified at level 5.
    EGIDS Level 6a (Vigorous)
        •  At this level, intergenerational oral or face-to-face transmission of the language is intact
         and widespread in the community. The language use and transmission situation is stable
           or gaining strength. At this level, the vast majority of adults, parents, grandparents, and
           great grandparents are using the language and making it possible for children to acquire
         and use the language for everyday communication. In most cases intergenerational
           transmission happens naturally in the home and neighborhood and is not dependent on
           schools or other more formal mechanisms outside of the “home and hearth.” Sign
          languages constitute a special case in that the acquisition of a sign language most often
           occurs in Deaf schools, especially when a deaf child has hearing parents.
        •  Languages with vigorous face-to-face use and clearly identified functional assignments
           within a speech community can remain in use for many generations. As described in
           chapter 4, stable multilingualism provides the ecological setting for sustainable use.
    EGIDS Level 6b (Threatened)
        •  This is the level of face-to-face use that indicates the beginnings of erosion in language
            use. Level 6a represents a stable multilingual configuration as described in chapter 4
         where informal functions are assigned to the Low language and more formal functions are
           assigned to the High variety. In contrast, Level 6b represents the loss of that stable
          arrangement with the informal domains being overtaken by another language or
           languages. At Level 6b, a large number of parents continue to transmit the language to
            their children even while a significant number do not, so that intergenerational
           transmission is weakening. With each new generation, there will be fewer speakers or
          fewer domains of use or both. At this level, there may only be barely discernible portents
            of language shift and few in the community may have any sense of impending danger.
         EGIDS 6b is the first of the EGIDS levels that is not considered “safe” according to the
             criteria used by UNESCO.
    EGIDS Level 7 (Shifting)
        •  This is the level that identifies clear cases of language shift in progress. The fact that
           parents are not passing the language on to their children is clearly discernible and has
         become the norm within the language community. Consequently the number of domains
         where use of the language is dominant are decreasing. Language revitalization through
           reestablishing home transmission would still be a possibility at this stage since the
          language is the first language for most of the parents and is in use among people in that
           generation and older. The language could be transmitted to at least some of the children
                if parents could be made aware of the need to do so.
H.2    FAMED conditions for sustainable use
The EGIDS enables a community to evaluate its current level of language use and the vitality of the
language, assigning it to a specific level on the scale. In chapter 6, we described the sustainable
levels of language use. The sustainable levels constitute possible goals for language development
efforts undertaken by local language communities. In this chapter, we turn to the question of how to
address the sociolinguistic, sociopolitical, and socioeconomic conditions which affect the EGIDS
status of a language. The EGIDS level provides a useful shorthand description of the status of a
language. That status, however, encompasses a complex set of factors and conditions that are
interrelated. If a community wishes to engage in language development activities that will move it to
one of the sustainable levels of use, it must answer the question what conditions need to be in place
in order to achieve the desired sustainable level of use? This requires a more detailed analysis of the
situation than the EGIDS provides. Though the factors contributing to a language’s status are many

125

and are complex, they can be understood in terms of five general conditions, each of which addresses
an important component in determining the vitality of a language within a given speech community.
     Sustainable language use, at any level, can only be achieved if each of the five conditions is at a
level which supports it. The FAMED conditions are:
        Functions – Functions (uses, bodies of knowledge) associated with the language must exist
            and be recognized by the community.
         Acquisition – A means of acquiring the needed proficiency to use the language for those
              Functions must be in place and accessible to community members.
        Motivation – Community members must be motivated to use the language for those
              Functions. They must perceive that the use of the language for those Functions is
               beneficial in some way.
        Environment – The policy environment (including at national, regional, and local levels)
            must not be hostile to the use of the language for those Functions.
         Differentiation – Societal norms must clearly delineate the Functions assigned to the local
             language marking them as distinct from the Functions for other languages in the
             speech community’s repertoire.
